extracted.intended_audience: students, poets, playwrights, and literary/theatrical theorists
extracted.subtask_description: Classical guidance (from Aristotle's Poetics) on composing and evaluating tragedy, epic, and related poetic forms: what counts as a good plot, character, diction, spectacle, chorus, and the moral/psychological effects (pity, fear, catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament; represented by actors, not narrated; effecting through pity and fear the catharsis of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy should aim to produce the purgation (catharsis) of pity and fear by presenting a coherent serious action. The language, medium (drama, actors), and embellishments must suit this end; avoid treating trivial matters as tragic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Elements of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The components of a tragedy are: plot (mythos), character (ethos), thought (dianoia), diction (lexis), song/melody (melos), and spectacle (opsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are not equal: plot is primary (the 'soul' of tragedy), followed by character and thought; diction and melody are important; spectacle is least artistic though impactful. A strong tragedy integrates all six toward the single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (Mythos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the most important element; it is the structure of incidents and the organization of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot must show an ordered sequence of necessary or probable actions leading from beginning to middle to end; character and language serve the needs of plot. Evaluate a work first by how well its plot achieves unity and produces catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and Completeness of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must be a 'whole' with a beginning, middle, and end: beginning is that which does not necessarily follow anything else, end is that after which nothing else follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The parts should be so connected that removal or rearrangement harms the whole. The action should be single and unified — avoid multiple unconnected episodes or digressions that break causal continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are either complex (contain reversal and/or recognition) or simple (change without reversal/recognition). Complex plots are superior artistically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complex plot (with peripeteia and/or anagnorisis) creates a more powerful catharsis; when reversal and recognition occur together and are well-timed, the emotional effect is greatest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden change of situation from good to bad (or vice versa) in the life of the protagonist that arises naturally from the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal must be probable or necessary given the plot's chain of causes; when well-executed it heightens pity and fear and contributes to catharsis. Avoid contrived or arbitrary reversals that lack causal motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change from ignorance to knowledge, especially of a person’s true identity or situation, within the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition is most effective when it accompanies or produces reversal; it should arise from the plot's causal structure rather than deus ex machina revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (Error / Tragic Fault)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist’s error or frailty — not necessarily moral depravity — that brings about the reversal of fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The error should be believable and appropriate to the character; when misfortune befalls a character who is not wholly wicked, the audience’s pity and fear are engaged. Avoid making the protagonist wholly vicious or purely virtuous if the aim is tragic pity/fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be good (or at least not evil), appropriate, consistent, and lifelike; moral character supports the credibility of actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character is subsidiary to plot — actions reveal character. A tragic hero should have qualities that make their downfall plausible and moving; inconsistent or unbelievable behavior diminishes the work’s effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity for reasoning and the expressed themes — what the characters think and argue, including the sentiments and reasoning that the poem conveys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought is judged by the sense and persuasiveness of the arguments and by how well the speech advances plot and reveals character or theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (Lexis) and Style
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of words, phrasing, and linguistic ornament (including use of metaphor) appropriate to the characters and genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good diction is clear, fitting, and often involves apt metaphorical expression; verse-meter and appropriate linguistic ornament enhance the poetic effect without obscuring the plot or thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody and Chorus (Melos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The musical element and chorus should be integrated into the work as part of the whole action rather than an extraneous addition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choral song and melody can heighten emotional effect and should contribute to the unity of the piece. They are important but serve the drama’s action and theme rather than carry it alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (Opsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The visual staging and stagecraft of a production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle has great immediate impact but is the least artistic element because it depends more on the stage-craftsman than the poet; it should not be relied on to compensate for weak plot or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (Psychological Effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The purgation or purification of pity and fear produced by tragedy's representation of serious action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ultimate aim of tragedy is to arouse then purge these emotions; plot structure (including reversal/recognition) and credible character motivate this response. Assess a tragedy by how effectively it produces catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Necessity in Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the poem must follow by necessity or probability from one another; improbable or arbitrary incidents weaken the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causal coherence is essential. Even surprising events should be such that they could reasonably happen within the story’s world or follow from character motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Magnitude and Proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Length and scale should be large enough to be complete and unified but not so large as to lose unity; the magnitude must fit the single action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too long dilutes unity; too short cannot develop the action. Choose a scope that allows a full sequence from beginning to end without irrelevant extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs. Tragedy: Formal Differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and tragedy both imitate actions, but epic uses narrative verse, can be longer, is unrestricted by unity of time, and lacks chorus; tragedy is dramatic and staged, more concentrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing, note that epic allows many episodes and fuller narrative treatment; tragedy demands concentrated unity and the immediacy of performance. Compare virtues accordingly (e.g., epic’s breadth vs. tragedy’s concentrated catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy (briefly defined)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy imitates the laughable, focusing on human foibles and the ridiculous rather than suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though treated less fully, comedy should avoid cruelty and aim at a lighter depiction of error or vice; different standards of moral tone and effect apply than for tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Metaphor and Poetic Ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Figurative language and well-chosen metaphors are marks of poetic excellence and dignity of style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor reveals insight and improves diction; ornament should never obscure sense or weaken the plot. Evaluate style for aptness, clarity, and intellectual vigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of Reversal and Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The placement of peripeteia and anagnorisis within the plot is crucial to the emotional effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-timed recognition or reversal (especially when combined) amplifies catharsis. Recognitions that come too late or reversals that are poorly prepared reduce dramatic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Episodic Arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of loosely connected episodes that do not form a single causal action is a weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodic structure undermines unity and thus weakens cathartic effect; prefer causally linked incidents that contribute to the single, central dramatic action.
